passage: You want the honest version? Fine. I'm Damini, I'm seventeen. Last year there was this boy, Pranav, and we'd been going out for a few weeks. At a friend's party he wanted to kiss me in the corner, and I didn't want to, not there, with everyone around. I said, "Not now." And he just said, "Okay," and went to get us juice. That's it. That's the whole story. But I kept thinking about it for days, because my cousin had told me boys sulk when you say no. He didn't. Later our school had a session with a nurse about consent and staying healthy, and she said a no or a not-now should be respected every time. I nodded so hard. I already knew what that looked like.

passage: I'm Ira. Ojas is in my biology class, and he's the kind of boy who makes jokes about everything. When our teacher started the unit on reproductive health and preventing infections, Ojas laughed through the first slides. Some girls rolled their eyes. Then the teacher put up a scene: two people, one says no, the other keeps asking. She asked, "Is the second person respecting the first?" Ojas stopped laughing. Later he asked a real question about where young people can get correct information, and she named the school counsellor and the local health clinic. After class I heard him tell a friend who had made a crude joke, "Not funny, man. No means no." I don't know what changed for him, but something did.

qa.q: Who did the teacher say young people could go to for correct information?
qa.a: She named the school counsellor and the local health clinic.

qa.q: What might Ojas's sudden silence during the scene suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the example of someone ignoring a no made the topic feel serious and real to him, not a joke anymore.

qa.q: What did the teacher's approach get right?
qa.a: Using a clear scene and a direct question let students think it through themselves, and she pointed them to trustworthy places for health information.

qa.q: How might the friend with the crude joke see Ojas after his comment?
qa.a: The friend may be surprised or embarrassed, since the class joker is now the one saying respect matters.

grounding: A classmate observes a teen becoming serious about consent and accurate sexual health information during a school unit.

passage: Mohit, you're sixteen and your friends are full of rumours, I can see it. Let me tell you one small thing from when I was seventeen, before nursing college. There was a boy in my tuition, Anil. We liked each other. One evening, on the way home, he stopped and asked, 'Can I hold your hand?' Just like that, asked. I hesitated, and he said, 'Okay, not today then,' and walked on talking about cricket. I admired him so much for that. Asking, and meaning it when the answer isn't yes. Now I work in a clinic, and I see young people hurt by myths about protection and infections that they picked up from friends. So, respect a no, and bring your questions to me or a doctor, not to rumours.

After the college fest in Delhi, Pradeep, sixteen, and his friend Eshaan walked to the metro.
“Did you see Ritika pull her hand away when I held it during the song?” Eshaan grinned. “She was just being shy. Next time I'll try again.”
Pradeep stopped. “Bro, she pulled away. That's a no.”
“She didn't say no.”
“She didn't say yes either. Remember what the health teacher said? Only a clear yes is a yes. Pulling away, going quiet, looking uncomfortable, all of that means stop.”
Eshaan was quiet for a while. “So what do I do?”
“Ask her. Properly. And if she says no, that's the answer.”
Eshaan kicked a stone. “Okay. Yeah. I didn't think of it like that.”

“Shalini-didi, can I ask you something embarrassing?”
“I'm a nurse, Aadhya. Nothing embarrasses me.”
Aadhya, sixteen, lowered her voice. “Girls at school say you can't get infections the first time. And that contraception makes you sick.”
Shalini put down her tea. “Both wrong. Infections can pass any time. Condoms help protect against pregnancy and many infections. Other methods exist too, but a doctor should explain those, depending on the person.”
“Okay.”
“And the most important thing isn't any of that. It's that nobody should pressure you. If you're not sure, the answer is no. You can change your mind any time.”
Aadhya nodded slowly. “Can I come to you if I have more questions?”
“Always. Or to the clinic. Never just the internet.”

qa.q: What is Shalini's job?
qa.a: She is a nurse.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel asking her question?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and a bit nervous, lowering her voice.

qa.q: Where does Shalini suggest Aadhya go with questions, and why?
qa.a: To her or to the clinic, never just the internet, because they can give accurate information.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when Aadhya asks if she can come back?
qa.a: She probably feels trusted and glad Aadhya feels safe asking her.

grounding: An older cousin who is a nurse corrects myths and teaches a teenager about consent and sexual health.

Last winter, my friend Gargi's grandmother died. At school the next week, Gargi looked so lost that I went to hug her in the corridor, arms already open.
She stepped back. “Not now. Please.”
I'm Zeenat. For a second I felt hurt. I only wanted to help. Then I remembered what our counsellor said in the consent session: a no is a full answer, even from a friend, even when you mean well.
So I dropped my arms. “Okay. I'm here if you want anything.”
She nodded. At lunch, she came and sat next to me, silently, and leaned her head on my shoulder for a minute.
That was her choice. It meant more because it was.

Biology teacher's note, Class 10 health session.
Today we covered consent, boundaries and sexual health. The class was giggly at first. I kept it factual: consent means a clear, free yes; it can be taken back at any time; silence or pressure is not a yes.
Sahil asked, "What if someone says yes and then changes their mind?" I said then it's a no, and a respectful person stops. Uma added, "Like when my cousin tickles me and I say stop, and he doesn't. That's annoying, and it's also not okay." The class went quiet, then nodded.
We also covered how infections and pregnancy can be prevented, and that a doctor or the school nurse can give confidential, accurate advice.
Next week: an anonymous question box. — Mrs Thomas

qa.a: An anonymous question box.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been feeling when he asked his question?
qa.a: Sahil was probably curious and a bit unsure, wanting to understand what happens if someone changes their mind.

qa.q: Why is an anonymous question box a good next step?
qa.a: It lets students ask embarrassing questions safely and get accurate answers instead of myths.

qa.q: How might Uma's classmates see consent after her example?
qa.a: They may see that consent applies to everyday touch too, and that "stop" should always be respected.

grounding: A teacher's note records a factual class session on consent and sexual health.

Dear Diary,
At Rukhsar's birthday party tonight, Yusuf and I were talking on the balcony. It was nice. Then he leaned in like he wanted to kiss me.
I froze. I like him, but I wasn't ready. My heart was pounding.
I said, "Not now. I'm not comfortable."
He stepped back straight away. He said, "Okay. Sorry. Thanks for telling me." And then he just kept talking about the cricket match, like it was normal.
I thought he'd be angry or sulk. He didn't. I actually like him more now.
I'm glad I said it. And I'm glad he listened.
— Afreen

In Valencia, Pablo and his girlfriend Lucía were watching a film on her sofa. They'd been kissing, and then she pulled back a little and said, "I don't want to go further. Not yet."
Pablo felt his face get hot, and for a second he wanted to ask why. Instead he said, "Okay. Thanks for telling me." He meant it. They finished the film holding hands.
On Monday, Lars asked him in the corridor what had happened, grinning. Pablo said, "Nothing you need to know. And if she says not yet, it's not yet."
Lars laughed, but later, walking home, he admitted he'd never been sure what counted as a yes. Pablo told him what the school nurse said in the sex-ed class: ask, listen, and a yes can change to no at any time.

qa.q: What did Lucía say when she pulled back?

qa.q: What was Pablo feeling when Lucía said not yet?
qa.a: Pablo felt embarrassed and briefly disappointed, but chose to respect her and felt sincere about thanking her.

qa.q: Why was Pablo's answer to Lars a good one?
qa.a: He kept Lucía's privacy and made clear that her "not yet" was final, which shows respect instead of bragging.

The biology teacher at Chinmay's school ran a Friday session with an anonymous question box. This week she pulled out Tarun's slip, though nobody knew it was his: "If someone said yes before, does that mean yes the next time?"
"No," she said. "Consent is every time, for every thing, and it can be taken back."
Next slip: "My cousin says you can't get an infection the first time. True?"
Chinmay sat up; his cousin had told him exactly that. "Not true," she said. "Infections don't count how many times. Condoms help reduce both infections and pregnancy. If you have questions about your own health, the school nurse or a doctor can talk to you privately."
Chinmay glanced at Tarun, who was writing something in the back of his notebook. At the bell, Chinmay said quietly, "Glad somebody asked that." Tarun went red and nodded.

qa.q: What did the teacher say about consent given before?
qa.a: Consent is every time, for every thing, and it can be taken back.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay sit up at the second question?
qa.a: Chinmay felt surprised and alarmed, because his own cousin had told him the same myth.

qa.q: How does the anonymous box help teens learn this topic?
qa.a: It lets students ask embarrassing or personal questions without being identified, so myths come out and get corrected.
